paragraphs: Sometimes an exact proportion cannot be established among the constituent parts of the State, or causes that cannot be removed keep altering the relation of one part to another. In that case the remedy is to set up a special magistracy that forms no corporate unity with the rest. It restores to each term its right relation to the others, and it provides a link, or middle term, between prince and people, or between prince and Sovereign, or, if necessary, between all three at once.

I shall call this body the _tribunate_. It is the preserver of the laws and of the legislative power. Sometimes it serves to protect the Sovereign against the government, as the tribunes of the people did at Rome. Sometimes it supports the government against the people, as the Council of Ten now does at Venice. And sometimes it maintains the balance between the two, as the Ephors did at Sparta.

The tribunate is not a constituent part of the city, and it should have no share in either legislative or executive power. But this very fact makes its own power greater, for although it can do nothing, it can prevent anything from being done. As the defender of the laws, it is more sacred and more revered than the prince who carries them out, or the Sovereign who enacts them. This was seen very clearly at Rome, where the proud patricians, for all their scorn of the people, were forced to bow before one of its officers, who had neither auspices nor jurisdiction.

A tribunate that is wisely tempered is the strongest support a good constitution can have. But if its strength is ever so slightly excessive, it overturns the whole State. Weakness, on the other hand, is not natural to it: as long as it is something at all, it is never less than it should be.

It degenerates into tyranny when it usurps the executive power, which it should only restrain, and when it tries to set the laws aside, which it should only protect. The immense power of the Ephors was harmless as long as Sparta kept its morals, but once corruption had begun, it hastened it. The blood of Agis, slaughtered by these tyrants, was avenged by his successor Cleomenes. The crime and the punishment of the Ephors alike hastened the destruction of the republic, and after Cleomenes Sparta ceased to count for anything. Rome perished in the same way. The excessive power of the tribunes, which they had seized little by little, finally served, with the help of laws made to secure liberty, as a safeguard for the emperors who destroyed it. As for the Venetian Council of Ten, it is a tribunal of blood, an object of horror to patricians and people alike. Far from giving the laws lofty protection, now that they have been degraded it does nothing but strike blows in the dark, which no one dares to notice.

Like the government, the tribunate grows weaker as the number of its members increases. The tribunes of the Roman people, who at first numbered only two and then five, wished to double that number. The senate let them, confident that it could use one tribune to check another, as indeed it later did freely.

The best way to prevent usurpations by so formidable a body would be not to make it permanent, but to regulate the periods during which it stays in abeyance, though no government has yet used this method. These intervals should not be long enough to give abuses time to grow strong. They may be fixed by law in such a way that they can easily be shortened, when necessary, by extraordinary commissions.

This method seems to me to have no disadvantages. As I have said, the tribunate forms no part of the constitution, so it can be removed without affecting the constitution. The method also seems effective, because a magistrate newly restored starts out not with the power his predecessor exercised, but with the power the law allows him.
